faq.q1: How do I calculate a percentage of a number?
faq.a1: Multiply the number by the percentage and divide by 100. For example, 15% of 200 = 200 × 15 ÷ 100 = 30.
faq.q2: How do I find what percent one number is of another?
faq.a2: Divide the first number by the second and multiply by 100. For example, 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%.
faq.q3: How do I calculate percentage increase or decrease?
faq.a3: Subtract the starting value from the final value, divide by the absolute value of the starting value, and multiply by 100. A positive result is an increase, a negative one is a decrease.
faq.q4: How do I add or subtract a percentage?
faq.a4: To add a percentage, multiply the number by (1 + percent / 100). To subtract, use (1 minus percent / 100). For example, 200 + 15% = 200 × 1.15 = 230.
faq.q5: How do I extract VAT from a total?
faq.a5: Divide the gross amount by (1 + rate / 100). For example, 120 at 20%: 120 ÷ 1.20 = 100 — that is the net amount.
faq.q6: Can I use decimals in this calculator?
faq.a6: Yes. All fields accept decimal values, and results are shown with up to four decimal places.

faq.q1: How is a monthly loan payment calculated?
faq.a1: Lenders use the annuity formula: PMT = P × r × (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1), where P is the principal, r is the monthly interest rate, and n is the number of monthly payments. Each payment covers interest first, then principal.
faq.q2: What is the formula for monthly payment?
faq.a2: Monthly payment = P × r × (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1). For a 200,000 loan at 6% annual over 30 years, r = 0.005 and n = 360, giving a payment of about 1,199 per month.
faq.q3: Does a longer term mean a lower payment?
faq.a3: Yes. A longer term spreads payments over more months, lowering the monthly amount — but you end up paying more total interest. Always compare both dimensions before choosing a term.
faq.q4: Does a higher interest rate increase the payment?
faq.a4: Yes. For the same principal and term, a higher rate increases the monthly payment. Even a 0.5% difference noticeably affects total interest on long-term loans.
faq.q5: Does the calculator include taxes, insurance or fees?
faq.a5: No. It computes principal and interest only. Property tax, home insurance, PMI and closing fees are separate — add them to the monthly payment for a full picture of your housing cost.
faq.q6: How can I reduce my monthly payment?
faq.a6: Three effective levers: extend the term (more months, less per month, more interest overall), increase the down payment (less principal, less interest), or refinance at a lower rate when possible.

faq.q2: What is the compound interest formula?
faq.a2: A = P × (1 + r/n)^(n×t), where P is the principal, r is the annual interest rate, n is the number of compounding periods per year, and t is the time in years.
faq.q3: What is the effective annual rate?
faq.a3: The effective annual rate (EAR) is the actual return over one year after accounting for compounding within the year. A higher compounding frequency means a higher EAR for the same nominal rate.
faq.q4: How does compounding frequency affect returns?
faq.a4: More frequent compounding means interest is added to the balance more often, so it starts earning interest sooner. Daily compounding yields the highest return, annual the lowest — for the same nominal rate.
faq.q5: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
faq.a5: Simple interest is paid only on the original principal. Compound interest is paid on both the principal and accumulated interest. Over 30 years at 5%, 10,000 grows to 25,000 with simple interest but over 43,000 with annual compounding.
faq.q6: Does compounding work against me on debt?
faq.a6: Yes. Credit card debt compounds, often daily. A 20% APR card with daily compounding effectively charges about 22% per year — which is why paying off high-interest debt early saves far more than the headline rate suggests.

faq.a1: Multiply the original price by the discount percentage and divide by 100 to get the savings. Subtract savings from the original price to get the discounted price.
faq.q2: How do I add sales tax after a discount?
faq.a2: First calculate the discounted price (price minus savings), then multiply it by the tax rate and divide by 100. Add the tax amount to the discounted price for the final total.
faq.q3: Is tax applied before or after the discount?
faq.a3: In most jurisdictions, sales tax is applied after the discount. You pay tax only on the price you actually pay, not the original price.

faq.q6: What is the difference between percent off and a fixed discount?

faq.q1: How do I add sales tax to a price?
faq.a1: Multiply the net price by (1 + rate / 100). For a net price of 100 and a 20% tax: 100 × 1.20 = 120. The tax portion is 20.
faq.q2: How do I remove tax from a price?
faq.a2: Divide the gross price by (1 + rate / 100). For a gross price of 120 and a 20% rate: 120 / 1.20 = 100 net, with 20 tax. This is the reverse of adding tax.
faq.q3: What is the difference between sales tax, VAT and GST?
faq.a3: All are consumption taxes on goods and services. Sales tax is added at the point of sale (common in the US). VAT is collected at each stage of the supply chain (common in the EU and UK). GST is similar to VAT and used in Australia, Canada, India, and others.
faq.q4: Is tax added before or after a discount?
faq.a4: In most countries, tax is applied after any discount, on the final net amount. You pay tax only on what you actually pay, not the pre-discount price.
faq.q5: Why is the tax amount different when I remove tax versus add it?
faq.a5: Because the base amount is different. Adding 20% to 100 gives 120 (tax = 20). Removing 20% from 120 gives 100 (tax = 20). But if you incorrectly apply 20% of 120, you get 24 — that is not how VAT extraction works. Always divide by (1 + rate/100).
faq.q6: Can I use this for reverse tax calculation?
faq.a6: Yes. Choose Remove tax (tax-inclusive) mode, enter the gross amount and the rate, and the tool extracts the net amount and the tax portion using the correct reverse formula.

faq.q3: How do I convert a monthly salary to an hourly rate?

faq.q6: How do I compare a contract rate to a salaried position?
faq.a6: Convert the contract rate to an annual figure, then subtract what the employer would have paid in benefits, payroll taxes, insurance, and paid leave (often 20–30% of salary). A $60/hour contract is roughly equivalent to a $90,000–100,000 salaried role in the US.

faq.a1: ROI (Return on Investment) shows how much profit you made relative to the amount invested. Formula: ROI = (final − initial) / initial × 100.
faq.q2: How is ROI different from margin?
faq.a2: ROI compares profit to the amount invested. Margin compares profit to revenue. Both metrics are useful: ROI for investors, margin for businesses.
faq.q3: Can ROI be negative?
faq.a3: Yes. A negative ROI means a loss — the final amount is less than what was invested. ROI of −20% means you lost 20% of your investment.
faq.q4: Does ROI account for time?
faq.a4: Simple ROI does not. A 50% return over one year is very different from 50% over ten years. Use CAGR or annualized return to factor in time.
faq.q5: What is a good ROI?
faq.a5: It depends on the asset class and risk. A stock market portfolio historically returns 7–10% annually. Real estate often targets 8–12%. Marketing campaigns should clear at least 5:1 revenue-to-cost to be worth scaling. High-risk ventures should target 20%+ to compensate.
faq.q6: How do I annualize ROI?
faq.a6: Use CAGR = ((final / initial)^(1/years) − 1) × 100. For example, doubling your money over 5 years: (2^(1/5) − 1) × 100 ≈ 14.9% per year. This makes different time horizons comparable.

faq.q2: Is investing monthly better than a lump sum?
faq.a2: It depends on the market. Monthly investing reduces timing risk by spreading purchases over time and builds discipline. A lump sum can outperform in steadily rising markets, but carries higher timing risk.
faq.q3: What rate of return should I assume?
faq.a3: A globally diversified equity portfolio has historically returned around 7–10% annually over long periods. Use a conservative estimate like 6–8% for planning, and adjust based on your risk tolerance.

faq.q5: How much should I invest per month?
faq.a5: A common guideline is 15–20% of gross income for long-term goals like retirement. Start with whatever you can sustain, increase by 1% of income with each raise. The habit of consistent investing matters more than the initial amount.
faq.q6: What happens if I skip contributions for a month?
faq.a6: Missing one month has little effect, but regular gaps compound the loss. Skipping 10,000/month for a year removes that year's contributions plus all future returns they would have generated — over 30 years, that is over 100,000 in foregone value at 8% annually.

faq.a1: Income tax is calculated on your taxable income, which is your gross income minus deductions. The portion up to the higher rate threshold is taxed at the base rate. Any income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate. A tax credit, if any, is then subtracted from the total.
faq.q2: What is the difference between effective and marginal tax rate?
faq.a2: The marginal rate is the tax rate applied to your last unit of income (the highest bracket you fall into). The effective rate is your total tax divided by your gross income. The effective rate is always lower than or equal to the marginal rate in a progressive system.
faq.q3: Does this calculator work for my country?
faq.a3: Yes. Enter your country's tax brackets and rates manually — the calculator is not tied to any specific tax system. For multi-bracket systems, approximate by entering the rate most of your income falls under as the base rate, and the rate on the highest portion as the higher rate.
faq.q4: What counts as a deduction?
faq.a4: Deductions are amounts subtracted from your gross income before tax is calculated — such as retirement contributions, health insurance, or a standard deduction. Rules vary by country, so check your local tax code.
faq.q5: Why is my take-home pay lower than I calculated?
faq.a5: Most likely because of payroll taxes, social security, and local taxes that are separate from income tax. This calculator covers income tax only. Add social contributions and any regional taxes for an accurate net figure.

faq.q1: How is the monthly contribution calculated?
faq.a1: We use the future value of an annuity formula, solved for the payment: PMT = (FV − PV × (1 + i)^n) × i / ((1 + i)^n − 1) / (1 + i), where FV is the goal, PV is the initial deposit, i is the monthly return rate, and n is the number of months.
faq.q2: What return rate should I assume?
faq.a2: A globally diversified equity portfolio has historically returned around 7–10% annually over long periods. Use a conservative 5–7% for planning, or 2–4% for a savings account.
faq.q3: Does the calculator account for inflation?
faq.a3: No. The result is nominal. For real (inflation-adjusted) planning, subtract expected inflation from your return rate. For example, 7% return and 2% inflation → use 5% for realistic goal setting.
faq.q4: Is my data sent to any server?
faq.a4: No. Everything runs 100% locally in your browser. Your financial figures never leave your device.
faq.q5: Should I use a low or high return rate?
faq.a5: Use a low, conservative rate for near-term goals (under 5 years), because volatility matters more than returns. For long-term goals (10+ years), a moderate 5–7% is realistic for a diversified portfolio after accounting for fees.
faq.q6: What if I can't afford the required monthly contribution?
faq.a6: Three options: extend the timeframe (fewer months of pressure), lower the goal (smaller target), or increase the return assumption (take on more risk — not recommended for short-term goals). Extending the timeframe is usually the safest lever.

faq.a1: A fixed deposit (FD), also called a term deposit, is a savings product where you lock in a sum of money for a fixed period at a fixed interest rate. The bank pays interest, usually compounded at intervals, and returns the principal at maturity.
faq.q2: How is the maturity value calculated?
faq.a2: Maturity = Principal × (1 + r/n)^(n×t), where r is the annual rate, n is the number of compounding periods per year, and t is the term in years. Monthly compounding is the most common for term deposits.
faq.q3: What is the effective annual rate?
faq.a3: The effective annual rate (EAR) is the actual return over one year after accounting for compounding within the year. A higher compounding frequency gives a higher EAR for the same nominal rate.
faq.q4: Is my data sent to any server?
faq.a4: No. Everything runs 100% locally in your browser. Your deposit figures never leave your device.
faq.q5: What happens if I withdraw early?
faq.a5: Most banks charge a penalty — typically 0.5–1% off the applicable rate — and may also reduce the effective rate to the one for the shorter period the money actually stayed. Early withdrawal can wipe out a large portion of the interest earned.
faq.q6: Are fixed deposits safer than stocks?
faq.a6: Yes for nominal value — deposits are insured up to a limit in most countries (FDIC in the US, DICGC in India, FSCS in the UK). But returns often barely beat inflation, so the real (after-inflation) return can be low or even negative.

faq.a1: BMI (Body Mass Index) is a measure of body fat based on height and weight. It is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared (kg/m²).
faq.q2: Is BMI accurate for everyone?
faq.a2: No. BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat. Athletes may have high BMI but low body fat. It is a screening tool, not a diagnostic one.
faq.q3: What is a healthy BMI?
faq.a3: For most adults, a BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 is considered healthy. Below 18.5 is underweight, 25–29.9 is overweight, and 30+ is obese.
faq.q4: Does BMI work for children?
faq.a4: No. Children and teenagers use age- and sex-specific BMI percentile charts, not the adult categories. This calculator is for adults only.
faq.q5: Why is BMI different for athletes?
faq.a5: Muscle is denser than fat. A muscular athlete can have a BMI in the overweight or obese category while having very low body fat. For athletes, use body fat percentage or waist-to-height ratio instead.
faq.q6: Is BMI used differently in different countries?
faq.a6: Yes. The WHO standard uses 25 and 30 as cutoffs. Some Asian countries use lower cutoffs (23 and 27.5) because health risks appear at lower BMI levels. This calculator uses the WHO international standard.

faq.a1: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the total number of calories you burn per day, including basic functions and physical activity.
faq.q2: How many calories should I eat to lose weight?
faq.a2: A common recommendation is a deficit of 300–500 kcal/day for steady weight loss. For a TDEE of 2500 kcal, that means eating roughly 2000–2200 kcal per day.
faq.q3: What is BMR?
faq.a3: BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) is the number of calories your body burns at rest to maintain basic functions like breathing and circulation. It is the largest component of TDEE.
faq.q4: How accurate is this calculator?
faq.a4: It uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, which is the most accurate for the general population. Individual variation exists — track your weight over 2–3 weeks and adjust based on actual results.
faq.q5: How many calories are in a kilogram of body fat?
faq.a5: Roughly 7,700 kcal per kg (3,500 per pound). This means a 500 kcal daily deficit theoretically leads to about 0.45 kg (1 lb) of fat loss per week. Real-world results vary due to water weight, muscle changes and metabolic adaptation.
faq.q6: Why is my actual weight change slower than predicted?
faq.a6: The 7,700 kcal rule is an estimate. As you lose weight, your BMR drops, your body becomes more efficient, and you may move less (non-exercise activity). Recalculate your TDEE every 5 kg and adjust your calorie target accordingly.

faq.q2: How many calories should I eat to lose weight?
faq.a2: A common recommendation is a deficit of 15–20% below TDEE. For a TDEE of 2500 kcal, that is roughly 2000–2100 kcal per day for steady weight loss.
faq.q3: What are good macro ratios for muscle gain?
faq.a3: A common starting point is 25% protein, 45% carbs and 30% fat, with a 15% calorie surplus. Adjust based on your progress over several weeks.
faq.q4: Why is protein important?
faq.a4: Protein supports muscle repair and growth, keeps you full, and preserves lean mass during a cut. 1.6–2.2 g per kg of body weight is a typical range for active adults.
faq.q5: Do I need to hit my macros exactly?
faq.a5: No. Total calories and protein are the biggest factors. Carb and fat ratios can vary by 5–10% daily without meaningful impact. Aim to hit protein within ±10 g and let carbs and fat fill the rest.
faq.q6: How often should I recalculate my macros?

faq.q3: What is a healthy body fat percentage?

faq.q4: Does this calculator work for athletes?

faq.q5: Why do women have higher healthy body fat than men?
faq.a5: Women naturally carry more essential fat for reproductive and hormonal health — around 10–13% minimum vs 2–5% for men. Below these thresholds, hormonal and menstrual dysfunction becomes likely.
faq.q6: What is the most accurate way to measure body fat?
faq.a6: DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is the clinical gold standard, accurate within 1–2%. Hydrostatic weighing and the Bod Pod are close behind. Consumer scales and handheld devices are less accurate — often ±5–8%.

faq.a1: Ideal body weight (IBW) is an estimate of the healthiest weight for your height. It was originally developed for medication dosing but is widely used for general health assessments.
faq.q2: Which formula is most accurate?
faq.a2: None is perfect. Devine is the most common in clinical settings. Robinson, Miller and Hamwi give slightly different results — we average them to smooth out individual formula bias.
faq.q3: Does ideal weight account for muscle mass?
faq.a3: No. These formulas use only height and gender, so they do not distinguish muscle from fat. Muscular people may exceed their IBW while still being healthy.
faq.q4: Is ideal weight the same as a healthy weight range?
faq.a4: No. Ideal weight is a single number. A healthy weight is a range — usually derived from a BMI of 18.5–24.9 for your height. Both are useful as reference points.
faq.q5: Why are there multiple formulas?
faq.a5: Each was developed for a different purpose. Devine (1974) for medication dosing, Robinson (1983) for drug studies, Miller (1983) for general population, Hamwi (1964) for quick clinical estimates. All give similar but not identical answers — hence the average.
faq.q6: Should I aim for my ideal weight?
faq.a6: Not necessarily. Body composition matters more than scale weight. A healthy body fat percentage and waist-to-height ratio are better indicators than hitting an IBW number. Use IBW as a reference, not a target.

faq.q1: How much water should I drink a day?
faq.a1: A common guideline is 30–35 ml per kg of body weight. For a 70 kg adult that is about 2.1–2.5 litres per day from all sources, including food and other drinks.
faq.q2: Does coffee or tea count?
faq.a2: Yes. Despite the mild diuretic effect, coffee and tea still contribute to daily hydration. Most of your fluid intake comes from drinks and about 20% from food.
faq.q3: How much more water do I need when exercising?
faq.a3: Roughly 500 ml for every 30 minutes of moderate exercise. For intense training or hot conditions, this can double — weigh yourself before and after to gauge actual loss.
faq.q4: Can I drink too much water?
faq.a4: Yes. Drinking several litres within a short time can dilute blood sodium (hyponatremia). Spread intake through the day and do not force water beyond thirst during normal activity.
faq.q5: How can I tell if I am dehydrated?
faq.a5: Most reliable sign is urine color — pale yellow means well hydrated, dark yellow or amber means dehydrated. Other signs: dry mouth, headache, fatigue, dizziness, and reduced concentration.
faq.q6: Do I need more water in winter?
faq.a6: Less than in summer, but cold weather still dehydrates — cold air is dry, and you lose water through breathing. Indoor heating also dries the air. Drink to thirst and check urine color; the 2 litre baseline is a floor, not a ceiling.

faq.q1: How is max heart rate calculated?
faq.a1: The most common formula is 220 − age, which is quick but approximate. More precise methods include the Tanaka formula (208 − 0.7 × age) or a supervised stress test.
faq.q2: What is the Karvonen method?
faq.a2: The Karvonen method uses your heart rate reserve (max HR − resting HR) to set zones. It is more personalized than percentage-of-max because it accounts for your fitness level.
faq.q3: Which zone burns the most fat?
faq.a3: Zone 2 (60–70% of max) burns the highest percentage of fat, but Zone 4 burns more total calories. For weight loss, total energy expenditure matters most.
faq.q4: What is Zone 2 training good for?
faq.a4: Zone 2 builds aerobic base, improves fat oxidation and mitochondrial density. It is the foundation of endurance training and can be done for long durations without excessive fatigue.
faq.q5: How do I measure my resting heart rate?
faq.a5: Measure immediately after waking, before getting out of bed. Count your pulse for 60 seconds (or 30 seconds × 2). A typical adult resting HR is 60–100 bpm; athletes often have 40–60.
faq.q6: Do I need a chest strap or is a wrist monitor enough?
faq.a6: Wrist optical monitors are convenient and fine for steady-state Zone 2 work, but lag during intervals. A chest strap (ECG-based) is more accurate for high-intensity work, HIIT and Zone 4–5 training where precision matters.

faq.q1: How is the due date calculated?
faq.a1: The standard method (Naegele's rule) adds 280 days (40 weeks) to the first day of your last menstrual period. If you know the conception date, we add 266 days instead.
faq.q2: How accurate is the due date?
faq.a2: Only about 4% of babies are born exactly on the due date. Most arrive within two weeks before or after. An early ultrasound is the most accurate way to estimate.
faq.q3: What are the three trimesters?
faq.a3: First trimester: weeks 1–12. Second: weeks 13–27. Third: weeks 28 to birth. Each trimester has different developmental milestones and screening tests.
faq.q4: Can the due date change?
faq.a4: Yes. If an early ultrasound shows a different gestational age than LMP-based dating, your doctor may adjust the due date — usually only if the difference is more than 5–7 days.
faq.q5: What is the difference between gestational age and fetal age?
faq.a5: Gestational age is counted from the last menstrual period — the standard medical convention. Fetal age is counted from conception, which is about two weeks later. So at 12 weeks gestational age, the fetus is about 10 weeks old.
faq.q6: What is full term, early term and late term?
faq.a6: Full term is 39–40 weeks. Early term is 37–38 weeks. Late term is 41 weeks. Post-term is 42+ weeks. Babies born before 37 weeks are considered premature, and doctors may induce at 41–42 weeks to reduce risk.

faq.a1: A sleep cycle is roughly 90 minutes long and includes light sleep, deep sleep and REM. Waking up in the middle of a cycle often feels worse than waking at the end, even after less total sleep.
faq.q2: How many cycles do I need?
faq.a2: Most adults need 5–6 cycles (7.5–9 hours) per night. Athletes and teenagers often need more. Consistently under 4 cycles (6 hours) is linked to health risks.
faq.q3: Why add 15 minutes to bedtime?
faq.a3: Most people take around 15 minutes to fall asleep after getting into bed. The calculator adds this so your cycles line up with actual sleep onset, not lights-out.
faq.q4: Do I need to wake up at the exact cycle end?
faq.a4: No, but aim for it. A variation of 10–15 minutes still feels fine. If you regularly wake groggy, try shifting your bedtime by 15–30 minutes to land better in the cycle.
faq.q5: What happens if I wake up in the middle of deep sleep?
faq.a5: Waking during deep sleep (usually the first half of the night) produces strong sleep inertia — grogginess, disorientation and slower reaction time for up to an hour. Waking at the end of a cycle in light sleep feels much better.
faq.q6: Can I use this to plan naps?
faq.a6: Yes. For a short nap, aim for one full cycle (about 90 minutes including the 15-minute fall-asleep buffer). For a power nap, 20 minutes is better — waking before deep sleep starts avoids the groggy feeling.

faq.a1: VO2 max is the maximum rate at which your body can use oxygen during intense exercise. It is the single best indicator of aerobic fitness and cardiovascular health.
faq.q2: How does the Rockport test work?
faq.a2: Walk 1 mile as fast as you can on a flat surface. Immediately record your heart rate and time. The formula estimates VO2 max from age, weight, gender, time and heart rate.
faq.q3: How accurate is the Rockport test?
faq.a3: It correlates within about 10–15% of lab-measured VO2 max. Good for tracking changes over time; less precise for absolute comparison with elite athletes.
faq.q4: What is a good VO2 max?
faq.a4: For men, 45–55 ml/kg/min is good; 55+ is excellent. For women, 40–49 is good; 49+ is excellent. Values decline naturally with age, so age-adjusted norms matter.
faq.q5: How can I improve my VO2 max?
faq.a5: Interval training is most effective — 4×4 minutes at 85–95% max heart rate with 3-minute recovery jogs, 2–3 times per week. Combined with easy Zone 2 base work, most people see 10–15% improvement in 8–12 weeks.
faq.q6: Why does VO2 max decline with age?
faq.a6: It naturally drops about 1% per year after age 30 due to reduced max heart rate, muscle mass and capillary density. Regular training slows this decline to about 0.5% per year, and lifelong athletes can maintain near-peak levels.

faq.a1: Sleep debt is the cumulative difference between the sleep your body needs and the sleep you actually get over time. A single short night leaves a small debt; repeated short nights create a large one that impairs focus, mood, immunity and long-term health.
faq.q2: How much sleep do I need?
faq.a2: Most adults need 7–9 hours per night. Athletes, teenagers and people recovering from illness often need more. The ideal target is the amount that lets you wake up naturally without an alarm and feel rested through the day.
faq.q3: Can I pay off sleep debt?
faq.a3: You can recover some of it with extra sleep on weekends, but chronic debt takes consistent good habits over weeks to fully repay. A common approach is to add 1–2 hours of sleep per night until you feel fully rested.
faq.q4: Is my data sent to any server?
faq.a4: No. Everything runs 100% locally in your browser. Your sleep data never leaves your device.
faq.q5: Does sleeping in on weekends help?
faq.a5: Partially. Weekend recovery sleep restores alertness and mood temporarily, but it does not fully reverse the metabolic and immune effects of chronic short sleep. It also disrupts circadian rhythm, making Monday mornings harder (social jet lag).
faq.q6: What are the health effects of long-term sleep debt?
faq.a6: Chronic sleep debt is linked to increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, depression, weakened immunity, and cognitive decline. After 17–19 hours awake, reaction time is comparable to a blood alcohol level of 0.05%.

faq.q1: How is the daily calorie target calculated?
faq.a1: We use the Mifflin-St Jeor equation to estimate your BMR, multiply by an activity factor to get TDEE (maintenance calories), then subtract the daily deficit needed to lose your target weight in the chosen timeframe. The result is capped at safe minimums: 1500 kcal for men, 1200 kcal for women.
faq.q2: What is a safe rate of weight loss?
faq.a2: Most guidelines recommend 0.5–1% of body weight per week, which is roughly 0.5–1 kg for an average adult. Faster loss increases the risk of muscle loss, nutrient deficiencies, gallstones, and rebound weight gain.
faq.q3: Why is 7700 kcal used per kilogram?
faq.a3: It is the approximate energy content of 1 kg of body fat. This is a simplification — real fat tissue contains some water and lean mass — but it is the standard estimate used by most nutrition guidelines.
faq.q4: Is my data sent to any server?
faq.a4: No. Everything runs 100% locally in your browser. Your weight and health data never leave your device.
faq.q5: Why did my weight loss stall?
faq.a5: As you lose weight, your TDEE drops — less mass means fewer calories burned. Your body also adapts by reducing non-exercise activity (fidgeting, walking). Recalculate your TDEE every 5 kg and adjust your calorie target accordingly.
faq.q6: Should I add exercise or just eat less?
faq.a6: Both help, but diet drives the deficit. Exercise adds 200–500 kcal per session and preserves muscle during the cut, but a single restaurant meal can erase an hour of cardio. Prioritise food tracking, and use exercise to accelerate and preserve lean mass.

faq.q2: What is the difference between UUID v4 and v7?

faq.q3: Are these UUIDs cryptographically secure?

faq.q5: Can two UUIDs collide?
faq.a5: In practice, no. UUID v4 has 122 random bits, giving 5.3×10^36 possible values. You would need to generate about 2.7×10^18 UUIDs to have a 50% chance of one collision — trillions per second for centuries.
faq.q6: Which UUID version should I use for a database primary key?

faq.q3: What is ISO 8601?
faq.a3: ISO 8601 is an international standard for representing dates and times, e.g. 2025-01-15T10:30:00Z. The trailing Z means UTC. It is the recommended format for APIs and data exchange.

faq.q1: Can this tool verify JWT signatures?
faq.a1: No. Decoding extracts the header and payload, which are not encrypted. Signature verification requires the secret or public key and is not performed — this tool only inspects the token contents.
faq.q2: Is it safe to paste my JWT here?
faq.a2: Yes. Everything runs in your browser. Your token never leaves your device. However, treat your JWT like a password — anyone who has it can impersonate you until it expires.
faq.q3: What are the three parts of a JWT?
faq.a3: Header, payload, and signature, separated by dots. Header describes the algorithm and type. Payload contains the claims (user ID, roles, expiry, etc.). Signature verifies that the token has not been tampered with.
faq.q4: Why does my token show as expired?
faq.a4: The exp claim sets the expiration time. If exp is earlier than now, the token should not be accepted by any server. Some services still accept slightly expired tokens within a grace period — but that is server-specific.
faq.q5: What is the difference between decoding and verifying a JWT?
faq.a5: Decoding is just Base64URL decoding — anyone can read the header and payload. Verifying recomputes the signature using the secret (HMAC) or public key (RSA/ECDSA) and checks that the token has not been forged or tampered with. Never trust a decoded JWT until it is verified.
faq.q6: Where is the JWT usually stored on the client?
faq.a6: Two common options: in memory (safest, lost on refresh), or in an httpOnly cookie (safe from XSS but requires CSRF protection). localStorage is common but vulnerable to any XSS — avoid it for sensitive applications.

faq.a2: Both are permissive. Apache 2.0 also includes an explicit patent grant and a trademark clause. MIT is shorter and simpler. For most projects, either works — pick MIT for simplicity, Apache 2.0 if patents matter.
faq.q3: Can I change the license later?

faq.q5: What is the difference between GPL-2.0 and GPL-3.0?
faq.a5: GPL-3.0 adds compatibility with Apache 2.0, closes the TiVo loophole (hardware lockdown), and includes an explicit patent grant. GPL-2.0 is simpler and used by older projects like the Linux kernel. New projects generally prefer GPL-3.0.
faq.q6: Do I need a license for a private project?
faq.a6: For fully private, non-distributed code, no license is legally required. But adding one (even proprietary) clarifies ownership and prevents contributions from creating ambiguity. A short copyright notice is usually sufficient for private code.

faq.q4: What is the difference between HSL and HSV?
faq.a4: HSL (Hue, Saturation, Lightness) is designed for human readability — L=0 is black, L=100 is white. HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) is designed for color pickers — V is the brightest channel value, so pure red is H=0, S=100, V=100.
faq.q5: Which color format should I use in CSS?
faq.a5: HEX is the most compact and widely supported. RGB is useful when you need to adjust channels programmatically. HSL is best for creating variants — changing lightness keeps the hue and saturation intact. Modern CSS also supports oklch and lab for perceptually uniform colors.
faq.q6: What is a complementary color?
faq.a6: A color directly opposite on the color wheel (180° away in hue). Complementary pairs create maximum contrast — useful for emphasis but visually intense when used at full saturation on large areas. Use one as the dominant color and the other as an accent.

faq.a1: For normal text: AA requires 4.5:1, AAA requires 7:1. For large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold): AA is 3:1, AAA is 4.5:1. UI components and graphical objects need at least 3:1 for AA.

faq.q3: What counts as large text?
faq.a3: Large text is defined as 18pt (24px) or larger, or 14pt (18.66px) bold or larger. Most headings and larger UI text fall into this category.
faq.q4: Does it support alpha transparency?
faq.a4: The checker works with opaque colors. For transparent colors, composite them against the background first to get the effective RGB values, then check those.
faq.q5: Is AA or AAA required by law?
faq.a5: It depends on jurisdiction. In the US, ADA-based lawsuits often cite WCAG 2.1 AA as the de facto standard. The EU Web Accessibility Directive requires AA for public sector sites. Most laws target AA — AAA is a higher, voluntary standard.
faq.q6: What is the difference between contrast ratio and luminance?
faq.a6: Luminance measures how much light a color emits — a physical property. Contrast ratio compares the luminance of the lightest and darkest colors in a pair, expressed as (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05). WCAG specifies thresholds for the ratio, not for absolute luminance.

faq.q1: When should I use Base64 SVGs?
faq.a1: Base64 and Data URIs are useful for small icons and to reduce HTTP requests, especially for CSS backgrounds. They eliminate an extra round trip to the server and can improve load time for above-the-fold elements.
faq.q2: Base64 or URL-encoded — which is better?
faq.a2: For SVGs, URL-encoding (percent-encoding) is usually the better choice. It produces a smaller string and compresses better with GZIP and Brotli. Base64 increases file size by about 33% but is universally supported and simpler to embed in some build tools.
faq.q3: Do Data URI SVGs work in all browsers?
faq.a3: Yes. Data URIs are supported in every modern browser including Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge. Extremely long URIs can hit URL length limits in very old browsers, but for typical icons this is not a concern.
faq.q4: Is my SVG code sent to a server?
faq.a4: No. All conversion runs 100% locally in your browser using JavaScript. Your SVG code never leaves your device — nothing is uploaded, logged, or stored anywhere.
faq.q5: Can I embed fonts in an SVG Data URI?
faq.a5: Yes, but it is inefficient — fonts make the Data URI very large. The better approach is to convert text to paths before embedding, which removes the font dependency entirely. Tools like Illustrator, Figma and Inkscape do this when exporting SVG.
faq.q6: Why does my SVG look different after Data URI encoding?
faq.a6: Common causes: missing viewBox attribute (the SVG renders at an unexpected size), unencoded # characters in fill colors (breaks URL-encoded form), or external references (fonts, images) that cannot be embedded. Check the preview before copying — it uses the encoded string, so what you see is what will render.

faq.q1: Which regex flavor does it use?
faq.a1: It uses JavaScript (ECMAScript) regular expressions — the same engine that runs in every browser and in Node.js. Syntax is almost identical to PCRE, with a few differences in lookbehind, named groups, and Unicode property escapes.
faq.q2: What do the flags mean?
faq.a2: g finds all matches instead of just the first. i makes matching case-insensitive. m makes ^ and $ match the start and end of each line. s makes . match newline characters too. u enables full Unicode mode. y makes the regex match only at the exact lastIndex position.
faq.q3: Why does my regex find no matches?
faq.a3: Common causes: missing the g flag (only first match shown), escaping issues (\d vs d), or the pattern not matching the test text. Try toggling flags or simplifying the pattern to isolate the problem.
faq.q4: Is my data sent to any server?
faq.a4: No. The regex engine runs entirely in your browser. Your pattern and test text never leave your device — nothing is logged, stored, or transmitted.
faq.q5: What is catastrophic backtracking?
faq.a5: A performance failure where certain regex patterns (usually nested quantifiers like (a+)+) explode exponentially on non-matching input. A short string can freeze the browser for minutes. Fix it by making quantifiers atomic or rewriting the pattern to avoid nested repetition.
faq.q6: Are regexes the right tool for parsing HTML?
faq.a6: Almost never. HTML is not a regular language — nested tags, attributes and comments cannot be handled correctly by a regex. Use a proper HTML parser (DOMParser in the browser, or a library like Cheerio, BeautifulSoup, or jsdom) for reliable extraction.

faq.q5: What is a pronounceable password?

faq.a1: UTM parameters are short tags added to the end of a URL that tell Google Analytics (and similar tools) where your traffic came from. They don't change the page your visitors see — they just attach tracking information.
faq.q2: Which UTM parameters are required?
faq.a2: Only utm_source is technically required, but most tools recommend using utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign together. That combination gives you the clearest picture in analytics.
faq.q3: Should UTM parameters be lowercase?
faq.a3: Yes. Analytics tools treat Google and google as two different sources if the case differs. Stick to lowercase for consistency across all your campaigns.
faq.q4: Do UTM parameters affect SEO?
faq.a4: No. UTM parameters don't affect search rankings, but they can create duplicate content in analytics if used on internal links. Only tag external campaign links, not links between pages of your own site.
faq.q5: How do I use UTM parameters with Yandex Metrica?
faq.a5: Yandex Metrica recognises the same utm_* parameters as Google Analytics. Use utm_source for the traffic source (yandex, vk, telegram), utm_medium for the channel, and utm_campaign for the campaign name. Metrica also supports its own parameters (ysclid, _openstat) but utm_* is the universal standard.
faq.q6: What is the difference between utm_source and utm_medium?
faq.a6: utm_source is the specific platform (google, facebook, newsletter). utm_medium is the type of traffic (cpc, email, social, organic). For example, a Facebook ad has utm_source=facebook and utm_medium=cpc. Consistency matters more than perfection — pick a convention and stick to it.

faq.q1: What is the difference between margin and markup?
faq.a1: Margin is profit as a percentage of selling price. Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. They are related but not the same number.
faq.q2: Which one should I use for pricing?
faq.a2: Most businesses think in margins (what % of revenue is profit). Use markup when you know your cost and want a specific profit on top.
faq.q3: How do I calculate the selling price for a target margin?
faq.a3: Selling price = Cost / (1 − Target margin / 100). For a cost of $100 and 30% target margin: 100 / (1 − 0.30) = $142.86.
faq.q4: Why can't the margin be 100%?
faq.a4: Margin is profit divided by revenue. As margin approaches 100%, profit approaches revenue, which means cost approaches zero. You can never have profit equal to revenue unless your product is free to produce.
faq.q5: What is a good profit margin?
faq.a5: It depends on the industry. Grocery stores operate at 1–3%. Restaurants at 3–5%. Software and SaaS often 70–90%. Consulting 20–40%. Use industry benchmarks as a sanity check but focus on your own break-even and cash flow.
faq.q6: Should I include shipping and packaging in cost?
faq.a6: Yes. Include everything that scales with each unit sold — materials, packaging, shipping, payment processing fees, and any per-unit costs. Only fixed costs (rent, salaries, software subscriptions) are excluded from unit cost for margin purposes.

faq.a1: The point at which total revenue equals total costs. Below it you lose money; above it you make profit.
faq.q2: How is the break-even point calculated?
faq.a2: Break-even units = Fixed costs / (Price per unit − Variable cost per unit). The denominator is the contribution margin per unit.
faq.q3: What is the contribution margin?
faq.a3: Contribution margin is the difference between price and variable cost. It is the amount each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and generating profit.
faq.q4: What is margin of safety?
faq.a4: Margin of safety is how far above the break-even point your actual sales are. A 20% margin of safety means sales can drop 20% before you start losing money.
faq.q5: How do I lower my break-even point?
faq.a5: Three levers: reduce fixed costs (cheaper office, renegotiate contracts), increase price (if the market allows), or reduce variable costs (better supplier terms, less packaging). Each acts independently — combining all three has a multiplicative effect.
faq.q6: Does break-even analysis work for services?
faq.a6: Yes. For service businesses, the unit is often an hour or a project. Fixed costs are salaries, rent and software. Variable costs are contractor time, transaction fees and any per-project expenses. The formula is identical.

faq.a1: A payslip typically shows the employee's name, ID, designation, pay period, earnings (base salary, allowances, bonuses), deductions (tax, insurance, retirement contributions), and the net pay. Both parties usually sign it.
faq.q2: Is a payslip the same as a salary slip?
faq.a2: Yes. Payslip, salary slip, and pay stub all refer to the same document — a breakdown of an employee's pay for a specific period.
faq.q3: Can I add custom earnings and deductions?
faq.a3: Yes. Use the Add Earning and Add Deduction buttons to insert custom rows. You can name them anything and delete rows you don't need.
faq.q4: Is my data saved?
faq.a4: Yes, but only in your browser's localStorage. Nothing is uploaded to any server. Clearing browser data removes the saved draft.
faq.q5: Are payslips legally required?
faq.a5: In many countries yes. The EU Working Time Directive and most national labour laws require employers to provide written pay statements. In the US, requirements vary by state. Even where not required, payslips are standard practice and often needed for loan applications, visas and tax filing.
faq.q6: Can I use this for multiple employees?
faq.a6: Yes, but one at a time — the tool is designed for individual payslips, not batch payroll. Generate and download each employee's payslip separately. For a team, use dedicated payroll software that handles tax tables and compliance automatically.
